meta.title: Who really said "If you seek revenge, you should dig two graves, one for yourself"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Bezos said it on stage in 2016 — while quoting a proverb he doubted. Earliest known form: a Japanese saying about curses, printed by W. E. Griffis in 1876.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'If you seek revenge, you should dig two graves, one for yourself'?
meta.ogDescription: Not a Bezos original. He quoted it at Code 2016 and hedged the Confucius credit. Earliest known English form: a Japanese proverb about curses, Griffis, 1876.

answer.label: Not Jeff Bezos — he was quoting a proverb
answer.authorDates: Earliest known English printing 1876, in a proverb list recorded by William Elliot Griffis (1843–1928)
answer.sourceLine: Bezos really did say a near-identical sentence out loud — on stage at the Code Conference on 31 May 2016, asked about Peter Thiel’s funding of the Hulk Hogan suit against Gawker — but he introduced it as a borrowed line and openly doubted the Confucius credit attached to it. The earliest documented ancestor Quote Investigator can find is a Japanese proverb about curses, not revenge, printed in William Elliot Griffis’s The Mikado’s Empire (1876); the revenge wording is a later English rewording whose author is unknown.

source.excerpt:
Adapt the preaching to the hearer.

If you call down a curse on any one, look out for two graves. (“Curses, like young chickens, always come home to roost.”)
source.trailTitle: How a curse became a revenge quote — and then a CEO’s
trail: 1876 — Griffis prints it as a Japanese proverb about curses, not revenge, in his chapter of Japanese sayings: “If you call down a curse on any one, look out for two graves” (1876 first edition, Internet Archive ↗).

1915 — the revenge form surfaces in Peloubet’s Select Notes, still credited to Griffis and still called Japanese: “If you would revenge yourself, dig two graves” (transcribed by Quote Investigator ↗).
Mid-twentieth century — the proverb is relabelled Chinese, and eventually Confucian; Wikiquote now lists the revenge wording under its “Not Chinese” misattribution heading (Wikiquote ↗).
31 May 2016 — Bezos quotes it at the Code Conference when asked about Peter Thiel and Gawker, hedging the Confucius credit as he goes (Fortune, 1 June 2016 ↗).
source.excerptNote: As it stands in Griffis’s list of Japanese proverbs, with his English gloss in parentheses and the neighbouring entry for context. Note what is missing: the word revenge.

artifact.linkText: Read the 1876 first edition at the Internet Archive

source.rightsNote: Two different things here. Griffis’s 1876 Mikado’s Empire was published long before 1931 and is public domain — you can quote its curse wording freely. But the modern revenge wording on this page has no identified author or first publication: the closest documented utterance is Bezos speaking it aloud in 2016 while crediting it to someone else, so we assert no copyright status for this exact sentence rather than guess at one.

author.name: William Elliot Griffis
author.kicker: The man who put it in English
author.heading: Who actually wrote it down
author.metaLine: 1843–1928 · American orientalist, minister & author · in Japan 1870–1874
author.bio: Griffis went to Japan in September 1870, served as Superintendent of Education in Echizen and taught chemistry and physics at the school that became Tokyo Imperial University, leaving in 1874. His 1876 book The Mikado’s Empire devoted a chapter to Japanese proverbs, and it is there that the oldest known English form of the two-graves saying appears — as a warning about calling down a curse. He is the recorder, not the author: he presented the line as a proverb already in circulation, and the modern “revenge” phrasing is not his.

Modern wording of unknown authorship; quoted by Jeff Bezos at the Code Conference, 31 May 2016.

misattribution.heading: Three separate things went wrong here
misattribution.intro: This sentence has been re-credited at almost every step: the wrong speaker, the wrong philosopher, and the wrong country.

items.why: He did say it — at the Code Conference on 31 May 2016, asked about Peter Thiel funding the Hulk Hogan suit against Gawker — but as a borrowed line. Quote Investigator transcribes him as saying “It’s attributed to Confucius. Who knows if it’s really Confucius or not” before delivering it (Quote Investigator ↗).

Quote Investigator reports that researchers have been unable to find the statement in the writings of Confucius, and Wikiquote files the revenge form under its “Not Chinese” misattribution heading (Wikiquote ↗).
English sources from 1876 through 1915 present it as Japanese; Quote Investigator’s chronology shows it being printed as Chinese from a 1951 newspaper column onward (Quote Investigator ↗).

misattribution.truthLine: The oldest form anyone has documented is not about revenge at all: “If you call down a curse on any one, look out for two graves” — a Japanese proverb in Griffis’s The Mikado’s Empire, 1876 ↗. Who first swapped the curse for revenge is unknown.

context.heading: Why this one keeps changing hands
lead: A proverb with no owner is free to drift, and this one drifted twice. It began in English as a caution about cursing a neighbour — Griffis glossed it with the homely English equivalent about curses coming home to roost — and only later hardened into a line about revenge. Then its passport changed: sources from the 1870s to the 1910s call it Japanese; by the mid-twentieth century it is being printed as Chinese, and from there the leap to Confucius is short.

Bezos did not start any of that. Asked on stage in 2016 what he made of one billionaire quietly bankrolling a lawsuit to destroy a publisher, he reached for the proverb precisely because it was old and ownerless — and said in the same breath that he had no idea whether Confucius really said it. The internet kept the sentence and dropped the caveat, which is how a borrowed line becomes a “Jeff Bezos quote.”
context.detailsSummary: What Bezos actually said, word for word
detailsBody: Quote Investigator transcribes the moment from Recode’s video of the session as: “It’s attributed to Confucius. Who knows if it’s really Confucius or not, but: ‘Seek revenge and you should dig two graves, one for yourself’.”

Contemporary write-ups rendered the borrowed sentence slightly differently — Fortune printed “Seek revenge and you should dig two graves—one for yourself”, while the Business Insider report syndicated by Yahoo has “Seek revenge and you will dig two graves — one for yourself”. The popular “If you seek revenge…” form circulating today is another step away again.
context.pull: He quoted it, hedged it, and still ended up owning it.
